Commentary.Commentary: Here come the two English openers. 20 minutes to bat.

Less than 20 minutes to go for Lunch. England are well ahead in this game but in personal terms, this will be a nervous moment for Rory Burns and Dom Sibley. They would want to go into the break unscathed.

Another shoddy display with the bat for the visitors. This time it has been technical deficiency which has brought about their downfall. Playing from the crease, not shuffling their feet and getting trapped by the movement of the ball. Only Jason Holder played an innings of some confidence while the rest simply withered away. Dowrich's innings looks good on the scorecard but he struggled for a major part while Campbell got a brute.

So West Indies avoid the follow-on but England get a lead of 172. That is more than enough for a result if we get one full day's play. The bowling was pretty much upto the mark, except for that first hour this morning. 6 wickets for Broad, 2 for Anderson, but the entire bowling unit was excellent.

Stuart Broad takes the ball from Woakes and rightly so. He will want to keep that to himself. Not selected for the first Test and he has definitely made his point. 6 wickets in 14 overs, that is a wicket every 14 balls.

OUT! Caught! That is the end of West Indies' innings. Dowrich is the last man to depart and Broad finishes with 6-fer. Excellent stuff from England's talisman. He bangs the deck hard on off, Dowrich looks to pull but mistimes it and ends up lobbying it to mid on. Chris Woakes has a safe pair of hands and he makes no mistake. WEST INDIES ALL OUT FOR 197!

Broad goes up in appeal along with his teammates and the umpire agrees. Cornwall decides to take the review. Replay rolls in and Ultra Edge first shows no involvement of bat. Time for the Ball Tracker and it shows three reds. Cornwall has to walk back and England just two wickets away from batting again.
Review time! Rakheem Cornwall has been adjudged LBW and he has decided to take the review. Another one that looks hopeful more than anything. Let's see what the replays have to say.

They have looked a bit casual in their approach and have failed to bowl out West Indies before the follow-on. They do have the wicket of Holder but that is the only success they have had so far. Dowrich is still out there for the tourists joined by Cornwall who is no pushover with the bat. The visitor will like to bat for as long as possible. Can they survive another hour with the bat?

Holder looks to be plumb in front but has decided to take the review. More of a desperate attempt for luck more than anything. Let's see if he has any luck.

CAUGHT OFF A NO BALL! Big moment in this Test. Woakes has overstepped his line by just and Holder gets a lifeline. Woakes bowls a length ball around the body, Holder looks to flick but it does not come off the middle and ends up hitting it upishly to the right of short mid-wicket. Ollie Pope there dives to his right and takes a very good catch. Holder stays to see whether Woakes has overstepped his line or not. Replay rolls and it finds Chris Woakes guilty. Big let off for Holder as Woakes is very disciplined bowler. Chris makes a mistake and pays for it. How costly will this prove to be?
Holder is gone! But is that a no ball? There is some doubt there. Cannot say that there is something of Woakes' foot behind the line... IT IS A NO BALL! What a reprieve for Holder.
Good length delivery on off, Holder defends it off the back foot.

We are all set for the action to begin on Day 3! The England players are out in the huddle before they take their respective positions in the field. Overnight batsmen, Shane Dowrich and Jason Holder are out in the middle to resume their innings. Jofra Archer has the ball in hand as he will finish off his remaining over from Day 2.
WEATHER - A look at the heavens will bring smiles on all the faces of cricket fans. Dry in Manchester, no rain as of now.

All eyes would be on Jason Holder this morning. If his team can manage to bat this whole session, that deficit could come down to around 150. Still huge, but England would have to bat that much while longer to set a target of 400 or more.

To be honest, West Indies cannot depend on the weather. They are so far behind in this game, that just one full day's play can finish this match off. First, they need to score those 33 runs to avoid the follow-on and if they do, try and delay the inevitable by bowling tightly. But eventually, when they do get to bat, they have to play out of their skins, which is extremely difficult in the final innings.

So - why do we say will the Windies question the heavens? Because as per the forecast, there shouldn't have been much play yesterday. But we nearly had a full day's play! The forecast is for lesser showers today but if the forecast for 90 percent rain on Saturday did not prove right, what are the chances that the forecast for today will?

Another day in this Test match with West Indies having their backs to the wall. After the first game, such situations have occurred regularly in these two Tests. And now, having entered a Test with rain forecast for a major portion, the tourists find themselves questioning the heavens. Hello and a warm welcome to the third day of this third Test between England and West Indies in Manchester.

Okay then! We weren't supposed to stay up so late, were we? But for a change, the forecast in England proved to be false! We nearly had a full day's play with England probably just another full day's play away from winning this match and series. Join us on Sunday, 26th July, 2020 at 11 am local (1000 GMT) for all the action from Day 3. ADIOS! TAKE CARE!

The other English bowlers took inspiration from Broad. Especially Anderson, who came out all guns blazing. The tourists just could not find any breathing space and twice in two games, they are waiting with bated breath to see if some saviour bails them out of follow-on embarrassment.

Bowlers generally do well when they have had a lovely time with the bat. The Stuart Broad England loves, is back. The flashing of the blade, the pulling, the cutting, the driving - what not? And then he struck immediately with the ball too.

How did this all happen? The tourists began the day really well, getting 4 English wickets for just 18 runs, before Stuart Broad came in their way. Somehow, that 9th wicket partnership between Broad and Bess put West Indies off their track. From 280/8, the hosts managed to reach 369.
Right! So where were we? England on top at the end of Day 1. Where are we? England on top at the end of Day 2. First, with the bat. Then, with the ball. West Indies are in all sorts of disarray.

The umpires have come together and decided that the natural lights are not good enough for play to continue. The covers have also come on and that signals STUMPS ON DAY 2! It has been an excellent day for England. West Indies will have a lot to ponder over as they go back to the dressing room.

The two umpires get together again and they are worried regarding the fading light. They have decided to go off for bad light. The covers are also coming on. So that suggests that will be it for the day.

NOT OUT! Missing the stumps! England lose a review. Hard to be an umpire on this deck. A few overs back, balls were staying low. This is bowled from Chris Woakes a bit wide from the stumps and it comes back in to ping Holder in front of the stumps. The umpire disagrees to the LBW shout but England and Joe Root take the review. NOT OUT PLUS 5 RUNS! Full and outside off, Holder pushes it towards mid-wicket and sets off for a single. Dom Sibley gets across to his left, picks the ball up, turns and has a shy at the bowler's end. The ball hits the stumps and then deflects past the man backing up at mid off to the long off fence. Ben Stokes from second slip believes it is gone but replays show otherwise. Holder is comfortably in.
Chris Woakes is back and we have a Direct hit! England don't look that confident. Referred upstairs. Ahh... the big J is in by a mile.

FOUR BYES! Tough luck for Jos Buttler. On a length, outside off, Holder lets it go. But the ball comes back in a long way and seams past the off stump. Buttler dives to his left but cannot stop it. The ball races to the fine leg fence.
Jason Holder walks in next, with his side in awful lot of trouble.

OUT! LBW! More success for Stuart Broad. Huge smile on his face. Chase departs and the West Indies are 5 down. That looked as plumb as it could get. The nip-backer, as it is always called when Stewy bowls. On a length, outside off, Chase looks to stay back and defend. But the ball nips back in and stays low a touch as well. This is just Day 2, so cannot really blame Chase for playing back. Hits Chase on the knee roll as he misses his defense and there is an appeal. Not from Broad. He celebrates first, then as if like an obligation, turns back and asks umpire Kettleborough, who already has his finger up. Now now, Stewy, you don't want to be spending the evening in dad's office, do you? As per the rule, a bowler needs to appeal before celebrating, if it involves the decision of the umpire. Remember, the great Glenn McGrath being warned, around 15 years back for not appealing? Coming to this ball, Ball Tracker shows it to be clipping the bails.
Full and outside off, Chase lunges and pushes it towards cover.

Good running. Chase works this through mid-wicket. Broad gets there from long leg, beating Bess from mid-wicket. He looks to slide but slips instead. Stumbles but manages to stop the ball. Three runs taken.

EDGED, SHORT! Playing with soft hands is the key. Full and outside off, Chase commits into the defense but not completely. It is a mere push, more of a dead-bat, so that even if it is an outside edge, it won't carry behind. And it doesn't. Ben Stokes at second slip cannot quite get his hands to stop the ball and it goes past him. Two runs taken.

More on the Blackwood LBW which was turned down. Michael Holding was pretty much happy with the decision reversal. He feels that to the naked eye, his naked eye that is, the ball seemed to be going down leg. Now, if it had been clipping the leg stump, in this case, it would have been out. But what if Michael Gough had not given it out? Then it would have been not out. So the point of Holding here, is that umpire's call should be removed. If it is hitting the stumps, it is out, else, it is not. Fair point, aye?

Jermaine already has one overturned but just goes to show, small changes in things, like stance, technique, etc... can make a lot of difference.

We are back for the final session of Day 2. The England players are out in the middle. Roston Chase and Shamarh Brooks will resume their batting for West Indies. James Anderson will start the proceedings for the final session of Day 2.
... Day 2, Session 3 ...

310 is the trail for West Indies at the moment but look at the overs remaining for this day. 39 overs pending. If light holds good, we might still fall short by 10 overs, unless Joe Root and Dom Bess bowl in tandem to improve the over rate. This is the strong aspect of West Indian batting - its middle order. Can the tourists ensure that they not more than 4 down before close? The deficit can be ignored for now. Join us back at 4 pm local (1500 GMT).

England did reasonably well to make the new ball talk and should have got more wickets, but luck and their own fielders deserted them. They have mixed a good quantity of full and short stuff, keeping the batsmen guessing. West Indies tried to play normal cricket, with Campbell attacking and Hope defending, but losing both in the span of 30 minutes has hurt them.

Heartening to hear the conversation between Ebony Rainford Brent and Michael Holding on air. For the record, Holding finished his Test career with 249 Test wickets. On being asked by Ebony as to how does he feel on not being able to touch 250, Mikey says that he does not feel anything, as 250 is just a number. He further adds that plenty of people ask him whether he could have played more games to get to 250 but he curtly says ,'No, thank you!' Ebony tries to convince him that it could have perhaps been just one more game but Holding serenely replies - 'If it is a win for West Indies, then 250 is better than 249. Else not.' Ends by saying that numbers need context, else they do not matter. Gives an example that someone might have taken 1000 wickets but in 500 games. What's the use? Hats off to the legend. Are milestone dreamers listening?

While aiming to swing the ball, it is very important to have the correct wrist position. If you have pace, it helps but even if you don't, wrist position gives you great success. The seam should be upright, pointing towards the position. The masters of swing, like Jimmy, Bhuvneshwar, Starc, etc... do it perfectly. Broad is not a swing bowler, hence, he was not given the new ball in the middle stages of his career. Also, he just used to come and bang the ball on the deck, which is a total waste of the new cherry. But of late, this new Broad has started to keep the ball much fuller and hence, he has managed to get some movement.
